name: Carla Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a bulldozer at Hollow Creek, a big open-pit bauxite mine. Bauxite's the red rock they make aluminium from. I push the topsoil and rock aside so the diggers can get at the ore, and I keep the haul roads level. I'm out of the house by half five, home by six, and Wednesdays I go straight to choir practice. I love being outside on a big machine. What I hate is the new tablet in the cab that beeps at me every time I go a centimetre off the plan.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a little about home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Mark's a builder, his own business, mostly extensions and sheds. We've got Daniel, who's fourteen, and Ruth, who's ten. We don't owe money on anything except the house, and we've got a good year's worth saved, plus a share of my parents' old farm. My mum always said never borrow what you can't pay back by Christmas, and I mostly live by that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. At work I'd tell the young ones that all that talk was just talk. I don't do social media, so that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think it's what I always believed. People who build these things have never pushed dirt for a living. They think everything's a computer problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep working, keep saving, keep my head down. Mark and I would keep paying the house off early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, honestly. Things carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the tablet that beeps at you. How do you get on with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I put up with it. It's supposed to keep me on the plan, but I've been doing this fourteen years and I know where the edge of the bench is. I ignore it half the time and nobody's complained yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use AI tools, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I don't see the need. If I want to know something I ask Mark or I ask someone who knows. I don't want a machine talking to me like it's my friend.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised and tell the young ones at work that all the talk was just talk. I don't use social media, so that's where it ends.
S0.think: It's what I always believed. The people who build these things have never pushed dirt for a living and think everything's a computer problem.
S0.do: Keeps working, keeps saving and keeps her head down. Keeps paying the house off early with her husband.
S0.feel: Calm and pleased that things carry on.
S0.quote: I don't want a machine talking to me like it's my friend.
S0.fieldNote: Carla is relieved and slightly vindicated, with a clear distrust of the people building AI. She treats the dozer's guidance tablet as something to tolerate and quietly ignore. Her family's dislike of debt shapes her calm as much as her savings do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people have to work hard and look after their own. I'd tell the crew to keep their skills sharp and not wait for anyone to save them. I'd say it after church too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried. They're already testing a dozer that drives itself on the far side of the pit, and it does a tidy job. If that spreads, I'm one of many who could go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as hard as I can and make sure I'm one of the best on the crew. I'd save more, put off the caravan Mark wants. I wouldn't do any courses on computers, I'm not built for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared yet, but I'd be keeping my eye on that far side of the pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to be one of the best on the crew. Are you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm about in the middle. I'm steady and safe, but there are two young ones who are faster. I'd be pushing myself harder, and I'd be tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the self-driving dozers spread?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech companies, and the managers in the city who think a mine is a spreadsheet. Not the crew, and not the government either, really. They just follow the money.

S1.say: I'd say people have to work hard and look after their own. I'd tell the crew to keep their skills sharp and not wait to be rescued, and I'd say the same after church.
S1.think: I'd be worried, because a self-driving dozer is already being tested on the far side of the pit and doing a tidy job. If it spreads, I'm one of many who could go.
S1.do: Works as hard as she can to be among the best on the crew and saves more by putting off the caravan her husband wants. Refuses any computer-based courses.
S1.feel: Uneasy, keeping an eye on the far side of the pit.
S1.quote: They're already testing a dozer that drives itself on the far side of the pit, and it does a tidy job.
S1.fieldNote: Carla responds to threat by working harder rather than retraining, which fits her values but could wear her out. She candidly rates herself mid-crew. She blames tech companies and city managers rather than government or workmates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disgrace and somebody in charge should have seen it coming. At work and at church I'd tell people to look after each other. I'd not be online, but I'd ring around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think the dozer goes first, and so does everything else. Mark's work too, if robots can build. Our savings would last a year, maybe two if we were careful, and the farm land is something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything that isn't the mortgage, food and the kids' school. We'd use our savings to pay off the house in the first year if we can. I'd talk to my brother about moving onto the old farm with the family, growing our own food, and keeping chickens. And I'd lean on the church, because that's what it's for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot, and lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd lean on the church. Would you take government help too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, but I'd hate it. My family's always worked. I'd rather take a hand from people who know us than a cheque from people who don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel and Ruth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we're a family, we'll work it out, and God's got a plan. Daniel would want to fix things, he's like that. Ruth would want to know if the chickens could have names.

S2.say: I'd say it's a disgrace and someone in charge should have seen it coming. At work and at church I'd tell people to look after each other, and I'd ring around rather than go online.
S2.think: I'd think the dozer goes first, and so does everything else, including Mark's building work. Our savings would last a year or two if careful, and the farm land is something.
S2.do: Cuts spending to the mortgage, food and school, and tries to pay off the house in the first year. Talks with her brother about moving the family onto the old farm to grow food, and leans on the church.
S2.feel: Alarmed, praying a lot and lying awake.
S2.quote: I'd rather take a hand from people who know us than a cheque from people who don't.
S2.fieldNote: Carla's response to fast AGI centres on family, faith and land, not on government. She expects both her and her husband's work to go. Her reluctance about state support is strong but not absolute: she'd take it only if she had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for people to get ready, if they've got their heads screwed on. At work and at church I'd tell people to pay down debt and look after their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better. I'd be forty-eight, the house nearly paid off. Mark's business might last a bit longer, so we'd have something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save hard, paying off the house by year four. I'd help Mark with his business on weekends, doing the books and running the little digger, so we've got something that's ours. We'd start fixing up the old farm house in case we need to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I was doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd run the little digger for Mark. Would that be a full job one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If the mine goes, I could work for Mark full time, at least for a while. People still want a real person building their shed, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can pay the house off and get the farm ready. Two, we're scrambling. It's the difference between packing for a trip and running out of a fire.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time for sensible people to get ready. I'd tell people at work and at church to pay down debt and look after their own.
S3.think: Five years is better: I'd be 48 with the house nearly paid off. Mark's business might last a bit longer, so we'd have something.
S3.do: Keeps working and aims to pay off the house by year four. Helps her husband's building business on weekends with the books and a small digger, and starts fixing up the old farmhouse.
S3.feel: Anxious but feeling she is doing something.
S3.quote: It's the difference between packing for a trip and running out of a fire.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Carla builds a family plan around her husband's business and her parents' farm. She still avoids anything to do with computers. Her trust in people wanting a real person to build their shed is untested but heartfelt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so nobody should be crying about it then. I'd say that at work and at church. People need to take responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be fifty-three. The house would be paid off, the kids grown. I'd be able to finish out at the mine, then help Mark, and we'd have the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and saving. I'd tell Daniel to do an apprenticeship with his dad, not mining, so he's got a trade with people in it. And Mark and I would plan to retire to the farm, little by little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. But it'd be in the background, not on top of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do any training yourself in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd still not see the point. I'll do what I know until I can't, then I'll do the farm. That's enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young families at church who've just bought houses with big loans. They'd have ten years of payments and maybe no job at the end. I'd want the church to help them, not just pray for them.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so nobody should be crying about it then. At work and at church I'd say people need to take responsibility.
S4.think: At 53 the house would be paid off and the kids grown. I could finish out at the mine, help Mark, and we'd have the farm.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving, and steers her son towards an apprenticeship with his father rather than mining. Plans a gradual retirement to the farm with her husband.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the background rather than weighed down.
S4.quote: I'd want the church to help them, not just pray for them.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Carla stay put and plan a gradual move to the family farm. She stays firm about not retraining herself. Her concern for young indebted families shows a practical side to her faith.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There's no time to get ready and Mark's work would go too. What would help is the companies keeping people on for a while, a proper payout, and help from local people, not distant government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about what work means to people. It's not just money. It's getting up and being useful. If the robots take that, I don't know what people will do with themselves.

headlineQuote: It's not just money. It's getting up and being useful.
portrait: Carla Varga is 43 and drives a bulldozer at the Hollow Creek bauxite mine, with a builder husband, two children, a year's savings and a share of her parents' farm. She never uses AI tools and distrusts the people who build them, preferring hard work, family and church. She feels calm or uneasy in the milder pictures but alarmed by fast AGI, when she imagines both her job and her husband's going. Her plans centre on paying off the house, helping her husband's business and the family farm, not on retraining or government support.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there'd be no time to prepare and her husband's work would go too.
whatWouldHelp: Companies keeping people on for a while with a proper payout, and support from local people rather than distant government.
